extraction.name: XTREME-S
extraction.description: A benchmark to evaluate universal cross-lingual speech representations across four task families: speech recognition, classification, speech-to-text translation and retrieval. XTREME-S covers 102 languages from more than 10 language families, 3 domains, and includes datasets such as Fleurs, MLS, VoxPopuli, CoVoST-2, and Minds-14.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Ankur Bapna, Yu Zhang, Min Ma, Patrick von Platen, Anton Lozhkov, Colin Cherry, Ye Jia, Clara Rivera, Mihir Kale, Daan Van Esch, Vera Axelrod, Simran Khanuja, Jonathan H. Clark, Orhan Firat, Michael Auli, Sebastian Ruder, Jason Riesa, Melvin Johnson
extraction.citeAs: Conneau, Alexis et al. XTREME-S: Evaluating Cross-lingual Speech Representations. arXiv:2203.10752v3, 2022.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: XTREME-S groups several publicly available multilingual speech datasets and also includes a new dataset, Fleurs, in 102 languages. For Fleurs-ASR, the authors use 2009 n-way parallel sentences from the FLoRes dev and devtest publicly available sets in 102 languages, collect between one and three recordings for each sentence (2.3 on average), and build new train-dev-test splits with 1509, 150 and 350 sentences for train, dev and test respectively. Speakers of the train sets are different from speakers in the dev/test sets. MLS uses the official 10-hour splits from Multilingual LibriSpeech. VoxPopuli uses the 14 languages with more than 10 hours of ASR data. CoVoST-2 uses all 21 language pairs into English. Minds-14 merges monolingual datasets into a single multilingual dataset with a 30-20-50% train-dev-test split. For Fleurs retrieval, the pool of transcription candidates is augmented with 100k sentences from Wikipedia.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: FLEURS is described as complete at more than 97%. The paper notes that some slight improvements and changes may be done in a second version of the dataset, for example missing recordings or replaced low-quality recordings.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The benchmark is built from publicly available multilingual speech datasets: Fleurs, MLS, VoxPopuli, CoVoST-2, and Minds-14. Fleurs uses 2009 n-way parallel sentences from the FLoRes dev and devtest sets and collected speech recordings for those sentences. MLS is derived from read audiobooks of LibriVox. VoxPopuli contains European Parliament speech. CoVoST-2 is a multilingual speech translation corpus. Minds-14 contains spoken data from the e-banking domain. For retrieval, candidate text pools are augmented with 100k in-language sentences from Wikipedia or CommonCrawl.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The benchmark combines multiple existing datasets into a unified evaluation benchmark. For Fleurs, the authors build new train-dev-test splits. For Minds-14, monolingual datasets are merged into a single multilingual dataset with a 30-20-50% split. For retrieval, target transcription candidates are augmented with 100k sentences from Wikipedia or CommonCrawl.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: When needed, the authors provide scripts to download and easily reproduce preprocessing steps. Fleurs uses collected recordings for FLoRes sentences and new train-dev-test splits. MLS uses official 10-hour splits. VoxPopuli uses the 14 languages with more than 10 hours of ASR data. For retrieval, all embeddings of the dev and test sets are computed together with target text embeddings from 100k additional sentences.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The benchmark relies on annotations from the underlying datasets, including speech transcriptions, translations, language identification labels, and intent labels. Fleurs consists of recordings of parallel sentences from FLoRes. CoVoST-2 provides translations from 21 languages into English. Minds-14 is an intent classification task with 14 intents from spoken e-banking data. Fleurs-LangID uses the same train, dev and test splits as Fleurs-ASR for language identification.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For Fleurs, between one and three recordings were collected for each sentence (2.3 on average).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Speakers of the train sets are different than speakers from the dev/test sets for Fleurs.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Code and data are publicly available through the HuggingFace platform. The paper states that results on the retrieval task will be updated in the next version of the paper. It also notes that FLEURS may receive slight improvements and changes in a second version of the dataset, such as fixing missing recordings or replacing low-quality recordings, and that updates will be made on their platform. Additional test sets may be added in the future, and more details will be added on the XTREME-S dataset card.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper explicitly discusses speaker identity as a factor in speech classification and notes that speakers are different between train and dev/test sets for Fleurs. It also reports language, geographical grouping, language family, and estimated number of speakers for the 102 languages.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that making speech technology available in all languages is important to give speakers of under-represented languages an equal voice on the Internet and the possibility to make their content and culture known outside of their language cluster. The authors hope XTREME-S will enable the community to build better speech representations in many languages and enable rapid access to data-efficient speech technology for all the world's languages.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper observes that results are much better on the Western European group than on groups such as Sub-Saharan African or South Asian languages, which can be explained in part by the larger amounts of unlabeled data in Western European languages from MLS and VoxPopuli. It also notes that speech classification tasks are prone to overfitting given the discrepancy between the richness of the input signal, including speaker, domain, and recording conditions, and the small number of output labels.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The tasks are focused particularly on linguistic aspects of speech, while nonlinguistic or paralinguistic aspects relevant to speech synthesis or voice conversion are not evaluated. Test sets are open-source and not hidden to the public, so users are asked to avoid inadvertently overfitting on the test set. For speech classification, avoiding overfitting on speaker ID is essential. The paper also notes remaining gaps between language groups and that FLEURS is complete at more than 97%, with some missing or low-quality recordings possibly to be fixed later.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: XTREME-S is intended as an evaluation benchmark for multilingual speech representation learning and cross-lingual transfer. It supports evaluation across speech recognition, speech translation, speech classification, and optional speech retrieval. The benchmark includes train, dev, and test splits for fine-tuning and evaluation. The paper encourages multilingual fine-tuning, reporting average results over tasks, using dev sets for hyperparameter search and checkpoint selection, and reporting test performance. It specifies that at fine-tuning time submissions should leverage only the supervision of each task, with some allowances for additional unlabeled data and explicitly documented external resources.
